title: Catherine and Alexandru
description: Catherine vanished in the nineties; does she live? And who is the mysterious Alexandru, really? A missing girl, unrequited love and a vampire in London.
bodyHtml:
When the Carpathian Alps fell to the Red Army soviet agents searched the castle in the mountains looking for the young aristocrat who had partied with the Nazis. They found only one elderly servant who under torture revealed his master had fled west weeks earlier. The agents shot the old man and made their reports thinking the matter closed.



I met Alexandru in the Coach and Horses in Soho in ninety-eight on a winter night. I was with some friends - Catherine who at the time I had a massive crush on, David her boyfriend and the rest of our nightclubbing raving gang. That night we were drinking in Soho, taking a night off from pills and skunk. I always liked those old pubs with their history and cosy feel, particularly on a dark and bitterly cold night like that one.

I don't know how Alexandru ended up at our table but he must have been speaking to one of the others at the bar. He was perhaps in his early twenties, the same age as us and handsome with long dark hair and blue eyes that glinted with mischievous delight. He appeared something of an eccentric dressed like a rakish older man his black tie around his neck and dinner jacket open - quite the contrast with our jeans and hoodies. Alexandru told us he'd been to the theatre and loved going on his own - always something Shakespeare, always something bloody he joked.

Alexandru bought all the drinks (though I never saw him touch the glass of wine in front of him) and was generous with his self-deprecating wit.  As last orders were called he said he knew of a place nearby we could keep drinking and have a smoke if we wanted. We readily consented to this continuation of the fun and made our way through the maze of dark streets to join a small queue of revellers at the end of a cul-de-sac.

Our new friend told us that this place had once been a cinema back in the sleazy days of Soho but had been taken over by some enterprising young men who had turned it into a private members drinking club. He explained that at the door we had to say we wanted to become members but a fake name and a little cash (which he of course would provide) was all that was needed to gain entry.

Passing through the small and gloomy entrance we signed our new names and were presented yellow members cards that two spinning records printed upon them and the legend “The Social Club.” Alexandru spoke in French to three big security guards with gold teeth and scars. I can't understand much French but I think he was making a joke at our expense and he made them laugh like a pack of hungry hyenas. 

Inside there was a bar the walls papered ironically with the torn-up pages of pornographic magazines, the fashionable and the drunk lounging about on battered sofas. Beyond there was the cinema itself, the chairs gone and replaced with cushions and lava lamps. The original screen remained but showing a sixties psychedelic movie for those who preferred a different kind of thrill. The room was filled with pungent smoke that hovered in the light of the projector and Alexandru told us we could buy cannabis here which they'd cut from a block with a cheese wire.

I couldn't place Alexandru's accent and so at the bar, I asked him clumsily where he was from. He told me to guess and I tried for Russia. He was immediately offended and told me that he was proudly Romanian and that the Russians had done terrible things in his country - that the old families like his had been murdered or forced to flee.

“In the mountains we, I mean my people were voivode - great lords shown much respect, now we are nothing, hunted like wolves.”

“You seem to have done alright Alex”

“Perhaps…I like London it is an old city..it sustains me.”

I was passed a big blunt and wandered about the place drunk talking to strangers and watching the film. Later I saw Catherine and Alexandru speaking intimately together on a sofa, with her boyfriend slumped unconscious in one corner and decided to call it a night. I left heading for the night bus and the hope of some sleep.



It wasn't long after that I got a new job and left London. I made new friends and lived a different life - I was trying to build a career as a computer programmer and a new city and a clear head suited me. There was the odd joke email from London friends but this was before social media and it was very easy to lose touch with people.

There was only one worrying reminder of my hedonistic past life.  A few months later Catherine's mother phoned me (she'd got the number from my parents) and told me her daughter had gone missing.

“I haven't seen her for some time, she doesn't really speak to me - maybe her boyfriend, what's his name, knows something?”

“Her old boyfriend or a new one? David isn't very well, he's in a mental hospital now - she was seeing someone else some rich foreign man, but she is very secretive about him.”

“Alexandru?”

“Is that his name - what do you know about him?”

“Just his first name and that he's Romanian - I've only met him once.” I gave her a description but realised how little I knew about the man.

I worried a lot about Catherine at that time and I was still secretly in love with her. But time passes and changes many things. 



And that was it, I heard nothing of Catherine or Alexandru for two whole decades and almost entirely forgot them until one night in twenty eighteen. By then I was back in London, the work and the parties had moved east and I was employed as a senior web developer for a startup. With male pattern baldness, glasses, comedy t-shirts and a real ale belly I looked the part - the average white man in tech.

The company was throwing a Halloween night in a club in Hackney and that was where I spotted him again. He was seated at a table with the CEO who was already coked up and gabbling at Alexandru in that way she did when she wanted to impress. He looked bored and was glancing across the room looking for a chance to escape when he caught my eye. The hair was now in a top knot and the beard was new but he looked just as young as he had twenty years before.  Still not quite believing it was him I headed over.

The CEO spoke first “Alexandru this is one of our devs Jonathan, Jonathan this is Alexandru an angel investor.”

“We've met,” I said.

“Really? I'm not sure I recall.”

“The Coach and Horses, end of the nineties.”

“Oh yes, that night in Soho it feels like yesterday.”

“I didn't know you were interested in tech Alex?”

“Modern inventions, they are fascinating no?”

“Yeah something like that” I replied; the CEO scowled at me.

“Have some champagne Jonathan I'll get them to send over another bottle”

“How have you been keeping Alex? You look good.”

“Oh, I wouldn't say that this new century is very fatiguing.”

Suddenly I blurted out accusingly “Have you seen Catherine lately?”

“Lately?” He smiled “I should say so - I saw her a few hours ago she was getting ready for a swim.”

“Then…then…then you two are still together?”

“Yes she is still with me…my devoted bride you might say.” he chuckled. “Why don't you come back and see her.”

“Tonight? I..I don't think-”

“-why not we can get an Uber back to South Ken. Yes let us do it now, I'm certain she would love to see you again, it will be like old times” He turned to my boss “What you are saying is fascinating please furnish my assistant with the details.”

In the cab, I tried to ask Alexandru some questions about the intervening years but his replies were always vague and he preferred to talk about his home country becoming almost poetic in his praise of the moonlit mountains and forests. I enquired how he had come to live in Kensington and he told me that he had it been a very hip and trendy place in the early seventies.

“Ah, there was Biba, the cavern club in Chelsea and the market - such pretty girls you would not believe it.”

“How old are you Alex? Surely you can't remember the seventies.”

“No, no of course not…I have been told such things.”

The car pulled up beside a terrace of large white townhouses with Corinthian columns and sash windows.

“Oh wow, you can afford this?”

“It has been in my family for some time.”

I thanked the driver before getting out and as I did so I glanced in his rearview mirror and strangely thought I could see only one of us on the backseat.

Alex led me into the house, it was darker and more claustrophobic than I expected with heavy brocaded curtains covering the windows and dust sheets over the shapes of ugly antique furnishings.

“Mostly we live downstairs” Alex explained “I am one of those terrible Eastern European oligarchs you read about in the Evening Standard who has excavated deep under his Victorian house to build a swimming pool and a panic room.”

“You have a panic room?”

“I am ashamed to say it is true” he laughed at himself “But come Catherine and the girls will be waiting.”

A metal spiral staircase led down into a surprisingly modern space with white walls, a red chaise lounge and huge metal lamps. Two young women reclined on chairs watching an old black and white movie on a giant flatscreen TV.

One of the girls glanced up at me “We've been waiting for hours and you bring us this?”

“He's not for you Lucy, he's an old friend of Catherine's where is she?”

“Lurking in the pool as usual.”

The other girl didn't look up but just continued to stare at the screen, she looked thin and hungry.

“Come Jonathan don't waste your time with these two. The swimming pool is through that door, down the passageway, she will be so pleased to see you.”

I stepped through the door past bedrooms and a changing room into a huge dimly lit chamber filled with a deep blue tiled swimming pool. The reflections of the water's surface covered the walls and ceiling in constant motion.  In the corner of the pool in the shadows was a figure of a girl - somehow I knew it was her.

“Is it you Jonathan? He texted me….it's been so long. Why don't you get in, the water is lovely”

“I don't have any trunks I'm afraid”

“Oh don't worry about that, don't be shy”

“No, it's ok…I'm…”

“I'll get out then” In a few short smooth motions she swam across the pool and pulled herself out.

She was just as beautiful as I remembered her, completely unchanged. 

“Come to me Jonathan I've missed you.”

Feeling ugly and self-conscious I moved towards her as she put her arms around me her eyes locked to mine. As she leaned in to kiss me I imagined I could smell the faint scent of putrefaction. And then we were falling backwards still in an embrace into the pool. The water was shockingly cold and woke me as if from a dream. Floundering I could now see the water was filthy and the room nothing but a flooded cellar. Rotting things floated past in the murky pond as she dragged me down her teeth biting into me.



Back in the lounge, Lucy asked Alexandru: 

“She's not going to keep him is she? He's pathetic.”

“No of course not, there is nothing so sad as unrequited love. But he recognised me and we cannot have that now can we.”

title: Bettiscombe Manor
description: The spectre of an African slave takes vengeance from beyond the desecrated grave upon a wicked Victorian phrenologist.
imageAlt: A weathered gravestone standing in overgrown grass
coverAlt: a weathered gravestone standing in overgrown grass
bodyHtml:
Nathaniel Pinney gazed at the portrait of his ancestor the third Baronet John Frederick Pinney with a mixture of pride and contempt. Sir John was dressed for hunting in boots, a red coat with a three-cornered hat balanced upon a wig in the fashion of the previous century. An ornate flintlock was in his hands and his dogs pranced at his feet.

“And who is the negro boy?” Nathaniel gestured to the figure of an African youth standing behind John in the uniform of a footman, carrying a brace of pheasants.

“That is Jacob Smith, your honour. The Baronet brought him back with him from his plantations in the West Indies.” Answered Jenkins the manor's butler.

“He made a savage his footman?” Nathaniel was incredulous.

“Jacob was raised a Christian and could read and write sir. I understand he was very popular with the staff and in the village sir.”

“Poppycock Jenkins” Nathaniel snorted “It is now well known through the twin sciences of eugenics and phrenology that members of such races are primitive, subhuman at best.”

“As you say Sir” the butler replied with the faintest hint of insolence in his voice.

“What became of this Jacob?”

“A sad tale sir. Mr Smith died of tuberculosis, his last wish that he be buried in his homeland in Africa-”

“Such ingratitude” snapped Nathaniel.

“Sir John concurred with your opinion sir. The young man was interred in the grounds of Saint Stephen's Church. But many in the village say his restless ghost haunts the graveyard-”

“-ridiculous superstition. To imagine even rustic folk could credit such nonsense.”

“As you say sir. The coachmen have placed the laboratory equipment in the study as requested, will there be anything else sir?”

“No Jenkins there will not.” As he answered a plan began to form in Nathaniel's mind and a wicked smile passed across his lips.

Nathaniel had come into the Bettiscombe estate by way of his uncle, the sixth Baronet who had died childless. A sickly, pale hunched man with a balding pate fringed with lank long hair Nathaniel had spent much of his life in the grounds of his college in Cambridge. A champion of Charles Darwin he had gone even further extending theories of evolution and degeneration to humankind. In his system of categorisation, it was the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy who were the most highly evolved creature upon the Earth - far more refined and advanced than the base lesser races and the criminal class. Nathaniel sought to prove his hypotheses by measuring skulls and comparing a primitive visage to that of the cream of English society. Such examples he published in monographs within his circle who wholeheartedly endorsed his views.

Of course, finding decent specimens often proved problematic. Nathaniel lacked the constitution to travel to Africa or Asia and those skulls he could obtain in a Christian country were often of unclear provenance. Now to his surprise at the old family home on the border of Dorset and Devon presented the perfect opportunity. The bones of a full-blooded Negro lay but a few hundred yards away in the village graveyard.

Nathaniel visited the church the very next day and accompanied by the grovelling vicar took a tour. Within minutes he had located the headstone of the footman inscribed with the verse:

I who was born a pagan and a slave
Now sweetly sleep in a Christian grave

To Nathaniel's surprise, fresh flowers and some trinkets had been laid upon the resting place – obviously, the villagers still held the dead man in high regard. It was clear it would not be easy to disinter the body without creating a fuss and perhaps worse still a scandal. The doings of the resurrectionists were still very much in the public imagination – Nathaniel could not risk bringing such associations to the family name. No, if the deed were to be done it must be done by subterfuge without any suspecting Nathaniel. And of course, the academic being unused to manual labour would need help.

The following week Nathaniel took the train to London to give a talk at a Phrenology Society dinner. Whilst in that vast metropolis of vice and sin he made discrete enquiries to seek out those vile enough to undertake the deed he had planned. He was directed to an insalubrious street in East London to meet in a gin palace with two low men of the very worst kind who plied the dubious trade of grave robbing. Mr Mendes a defrocked priest and Mr Clothier, a drunkard heartily agreed to Nathaniel's nefarious scheme in exchange for a crisp pound note and a box of snuff.

The villainous pair were to stay at a boarding house in nearby Yeovil then travel to Bettiscombe by cart arriving at St Stephens at midnight whilst the village slept. This would allow them to dig into the earth and retrieve the skull of the unfortunate African. Not trusting the two rogues to fetch the correct cranium Nathaniel agreed to meet them in the churchyard and direct them to Jacob's grave.

The appointed night was moonless, frosty and dark – the stars affording the only light. Nathaniel waited for accomplices shivering in the cold behind an imposing tomb of an ancestor. The church clock had struck twelve some time ago and Nathaniel nervously attempted to check his pocket watch again and again despite being completely unable to see the hands. Finally, after what had seemed an eternity, he heard the slow clip-clop of a horse's hooves and the turning of a wheel. Peeking out from behind the mausoleum Nathaniel could see two figures in heavy greatcoats creep into the boneyard tools slung over their shoulders.

“Over here,” he hissed. “I'll take you there.”

The pair of ghouls followed Nathaniel and stood before the gravestone.

“It has been some time, no?” Asked Mendes “Are you sure you don't want something a bit fresher?”

“No, I do not – this is the one and remember I only need the skull – but fully intact you understand.”

They grunted ascent and set to work, Mendes swinging the pickaxe to break the sod and Clothier shovelling it away. As they toiled Nathaniel held a bullseye lantern to illuminate the growing hole with a single beam of light. The two men cursed and spat as they laboured passing a bottle of cheap gin between them.

Just as the clock of St Stephens peeled two the shovel struck wood and Clothier frenziedly pulled apart the boards. “Buried treasure” he chuckled and held aloft a gleaming white skull, almost perfectly preserved.

“Sterling, even the lower mandible intact” gloated Nathaniel as he wrapped it carefully in a cloth and placed it in his bag.

Suddenly Mendes gave a startled cry, turned and fled blindly towards the gate. Nathaniel looked up fearing discovery by the sexton but instead beheld a ghastly sight. In the beam of his lantern walking the path towards him came the figure of a man dressed in a footman's uniform. A man but not a living man for although the figure walked it lacked a head.

Filled with dread Nathaniel snatched up his bag and ran headlong after Mendes. Behind him, he could hear cries of terror from Clothier still at the bottom of the open grave. Not looking back Nathaniel reached the cobbled road in time to see Mendes start his horse and drive the cart at a devil's speed away down the lane.

The Baronet was glad that his manor house lay but a few hundred yards from the church and despite his frailty made it in quick time back to the ancient pile. Locking the door behind with shaking hands Nathaniel tiptoed down the wooden panelled servants' passage and entered his study placing the bag upon his oaken desk.

He decided he must first come to his senses and stiffen his resolve, he poured himself a measure of brandy from a crystal decanter, drank it fast and then quickly refilled his glass. Nathaniel Pinney firmly did not believe in ghosts and was now certain what he had seen had been a trick of the light or a shared hallucination. Of course, being in the company of low-born hysterical papists he had become infected by their superstitious fears. Drinking a third glass Nathaniel now laughed at himself and turned towards his macabre prize.

He lifted the bundle from the bag and unwrapped it on the desk, the skull rolling out as he did so. Nathaniel turned to fetch his calipers – ready to begin the examination but as he did so he heard a sound, a sort of chattering emanating from the skull. Turning back towards it he saw to his terror the dismembered head now moving upon the desk, the jawbone opening and closing as if in speech. Standing and staggering backwards Nathaniel was unable to believe his eyes but the thing kept moving.

Slowly it rose levitating above the desk, its empty sockets becoming level with Nathaniel's eyes. Behind him the door of the study swung open and through it glided the headless apparition from the graveyard- he was now trapped between the two horrors.

Nathaniel fell to his knees and begged “Please I'll return you to your grave, I'm sorry for disturbing your sleep, truly sorry.” The mouth of the skull opened wide in reply and from it came forth a terrible scream of hate and rage that shook the walls of the manor house.

Jenkins found the seventh Baronet Nathaniel Pinney dead upon the floor of his study in the morning, his face etched with the marks of terrible fear, his hand clutching his chest.  You can see the skull to this day at Bettiscombe Manor and the local people will tell you with a shudder of its screams in the night for the man they called Jacob Smith still does not rest in his homeland.

title: Shenley
description: A housing estate is built upon the site of an old mental hospital but do the victims of the institution still linger to haunt the new inhabitants?
imageAlt: A brick hospital tower with arched windows and a pointed roof
coverAlt: a brick hospital tower with arched windows and a pointed roof
bodyHtml:
If you take the train from London to St Albans and look out of the window to the right, you might catch a glimpse of a tall tower above the trees. The tower is all that's left of Shenley Mental Hospital, the rest of the buildings having been torn down and the land sold with a new housing estate built upon it. My father worked as a nurse at Shenley for decades until he retired, and the institution wound down as "care in the community" became the preferred policy. He told us many stories from Shenley and knowing some of them I wouldn't want to live in one of those houses, not for any money.

Emma had not liked the look of the small, modern flat, cramped as it was together with others and directly under the shadow of that big ugly old tower. But it was as far as the meagre mortgage she was allowed would stretch and her parents had told her it was just a foot on the ladder. Although there was nothing on the estate except for a small corner shop and shabby cafe she could get a bus to St Alban's for shopping or to Radlett train station for her commute into her accounts job in London.

Emma had got a survey done on the flat before moving in, plus on her dad's advice a snagging survey specifically for a new build home. None of the reports had mentioned the unpleasant persistent coldness inside the property which must have been some kind of damp nor the faulty electrics. Since the first day of moving in Emma had experienced strange power surges. Bulbs popping, the fridge buzzing loudly, plugs sparking when removed. She had called in workmen to look at both problems, they'd seemed puzzled and made some vague suggestions – but Emma's budget didn't go very far.

And there was one other thing. At night sometimes she was awakened by voices. Or rather one voice, a young man's sobbing and pleading. It was a dialogue, but she could not hear the other person – maybe it was a phone call, or they spoke very quietly. The sounds must come from one of the other flats. But not those next to hers – the one on the left was empty and the other on the right housed a single Polish woman. Perhaps from upstairs, but it sounded so close as if the man was inside her flat but then these new buildings have such thin walls and ceilings.

On a pale grey winter Saturday afternoon, Emma glanced out to see a white-haired old man in a parker standing outside just staring upwards.  She waited for a moment and he didn't move. Unsettled she drew the curtains and turned back to her laptop.

That night things became very bad indeed in her flat. She was awoken once again by that voice full of so much pain, now desperately imploring, begging somebody to stop. "No please not again Doctor Simmons...I can't take it, not again..." The light inside her room was flickering and the whole building felt alive with static. The voice stopped speaking and began screaming a keening animal wail of agony. Emma knowing she wasn't dreaming now rolled out from the under the duvet and was immediately stunned by the cold bitter air in her room.

The scream was so close she was certain it was coming from inside her flat. Tearing open the bedroom door she stood in the small hallway facing the living room and kitchen. Icy air flooded towards her and the lights flashed and strobed. The screams were now punctuated by a loud bang like a great machine discharging electricity. Emma crept closer her heart pounding in her chest edging around the corner. The voice now fading to sobs.

There she could see just in the flickering lights a figure of a thin male hunched up into a foetal position, shorn head down, bare ankles and feet, his body covered only by a shift. Something glinted in his hands as he held it against his wrists, slowly his head moved up looking up to meet Emma's gaze. Instinctively she jumped back behind the wall and there was another cry from inside her lounge the lights flashed and then went dark.

She didn't know how long she stood in the blackness just waiting and listening. Finally, she moved peeking into the living room and throwing a switch. The bulb was gone, burnt out but she found another light working and looked around. Nothing had changed from the night before. She checked the front door – it was still doubled locked, solid, unmarked. Likewise, the strong double-glazed windows were closed, undamaged. 

Emma put her coat on over her pyjamas against the chill and sat on the sofa holding her phone. Three thirty-one AM, she could call the police...and tell them what? That she was losing her mind? The room seemed warmer, she made a cup of tea, switched on the TV and promised herself to speak to her Mum about it in the morning.

And that's how she woke at eleven the next winter morning, an old movie playing on the TV. She leapt up remembering the night and looked around the flat checking for signs of entry. 

As she checked the windows again, she glimpsed again the old man, again just staring up. Filled suddenly with anger she was determined to challenge this creep. She wouldn't be stalked and frightened. Pulling on clothes and boots she stormed out and towards the figure.

"Excuse me, can I help you? This is private property."

"Oh, I'm so sorry, I used to work here, and everything has changed – I got a bit lost."

"What are you looking at?"

"The water tower, it seems to be only part left. Sorry, I'm George, George Nazer." He spoke gently calmly with a soft voice.

Frail maybe in his late seventies, white hair, thick glasses George didn't look much of a threat. And from where he was standing the tower was in clear view behind her block.

"Is there anywhere to get a cup of tea now, we used to have a social club?" he asked.

"There's a cafe on the parade, it's not very good"

"That will do fine" and he turned and started to walk away.

"Hang on you say you used to work here?"

"Yes, for twenty odd years"

"So, you know the history?"

"Yes"

"Hold on I'll come with you."

In the dull cafe over big mugs of tea George told her all about the huge sprawling hospital that had once been here. How he'd trained as a vicar but lost his faith in God but still wanted to help people and so had become a nurse working with the mentally ill.

"That was the late sixties, and I was an idealist. The reality was very different."

"What was it like?"

"Most of the staff were Irish, many of them had come over in the fifties, done national service and then gone straight into nursing. Big rough men who were there to restrain the patients more than treat them. They liked the union and a drink and a fight – crazy bastards like Ted Griffin and John McCahill."

"But some of the doctors had some pretty advanced ideas. Psychiatrists had free reign to experiment back in those days. There was one South African doctor who let the patients run their own ward – it worked very well to everyone's surprise. And then there were others who were petty tyrants."

"Like Dr Simmons?" Emma blurted out, not even aware how she had remembered that.

"How did you know that name? Done some digging on the web?"  George looked wary.

"I just heard it..."

"It was before my time, but the others remembered him – some people shouldn't be given any power – let alone over vulnerable patients." 

"What did he do?"

"Well, there was the insulin therapy for a start, injecting patients and sending them into short comas. He continued to use that long after it had been discredited. And there was the electroshock therapy. Now it was common practice at the time and is still used in certain cases to this day. But the other nurses told me Dr Simmonds would use it as a punishment dishing out whenever he pleased out of pure sadism. There were a few suicides, and he was moved on. As I say it was before my time, but still quite a scandal when I started."

"This is a silly question, but did anybody think the hospital haunted?"

George laughed. "Well, you have to understand a lot of the men and women I worked with were from rural Ireland. Strong Roman Catholics and secretly believing in much old folklore – banshees and the little people. Some of them thought that one of the buildings had a ghost and didn't want to take night shifts there."

"Which building? The one Dr Simmons worked in?"

"Well yes since you should ask...have you seen something?"

Emma didn't answer.

"Well, I never did become a vicar but if I was, I think I might give this place an exorcism. I need to catch the train now let me write down my number if you have any other local history questions."

She took the piece of paper and watched him leave.

Weeks passed and nothing else happened and Emma began to believe it had been a strange nightmare. 

But then it started again. At first, it was the creeping cold filling the flat worse than any damp. And then lights flickering, the audio on the speakers crackling, lights dimming and then suddenly flashing into bright incandescence.

After several sleepless nights, Emma began to hear the voice again. A whisper, so, so quiet but getting louder. The sobs and the crying in the dark cold night.

Emma called into work sick and took to sleeping during the day. At night she tried barricading the door and sleeping listening to her iPod but stopped when she couldn't escape the feeling of somebody else inside her flat.

Exhausted one morning she pulled on her coat and plunged her hands into the pockets. Her fingers touched something – a folded-up piece of paper. Absentmindedly she pulled it out and opened it up. It was George Nazer's note with his name and phone number. Hoping maybe there was somebody who would understand Emma dialled the number.

 "Hello"

 "Hi George, it's Emma we had tea in Shenley."

"Yes of course, you sound a bit shaken – are you OK?"

"You asked if I'd seen something, well I have...well more heard things...maybe seen somebody – I think they were a patient."

"I understand. Would you like to chat – meet at the same place, say three this afternoon?"

Back in the cafe Emma haltingly explained to George what she had experienced, attempting to sound rational and avoiding any supernatural terms. He nodded, sipped his tea and listened.

"Do you think I'm going mad?" she asked.

"In my old work we didn't use that word, it creates a stigma. Do I think you are hallucinating? Possibly, surprisingly a lot of people do saints, mystics, and all sort of normal people alongside those whom we consider to be suffering from mental illness. There is an easy way to find out. Could somebody else stay there with you? Or could you stay with somebody else whilst another person investigates?"

"I haven't told my Mum she would never believe me and if she did, she would die of worry. You are the only person I have told can you come and see – I know it's a weird thing to ask."

"Why would you trust me? Isn't there someone else you can rely on?"

"I know it sounds crazy but for some reason, I do trust you."

"Crazy – that's another word we don't use."

At the flat, they ate microwave meals and watched some TV on edge waiting for something to happen. Once again, as it grew dark the temperature of the room fell, the image on the screen flickered and the lights buzzed. But the voice was not heard.

"Why don't you try and get some sleep?" George said "I'll make some coffee and read my book. I'm used to night shifts and besides at my age I don't get much sleep anyhow."

"What are you reading?"

He held the book up "E.F. Benson, ghost stories as luck would have it."

"OK then but wake me up if something happens."

For the first time in days Emma felt she could give into sleep and crawled under the duvet falling into an instant deep slumber. Then suddenly she was awake sitting up and listening. She could hear voices but couldn't make out the words. The pathetic voice still sobbed but seemed quieter and calmer whilst George in engaged it in conversation speaking in a soothing tone. Reluctant to interrupt them Emma waited and listened. The talking seemed to finish and then the sound of the front closing. Jumping out of bed Emma rushed out of the room hoping to find George. 

Peeking around the corner she could see the lounge and the kitchen; at the flick of the switch, the lights came on with a steady strong illumination. The room contained neither the old man nor the apparition. The air felt warm and peaceful.

Emma waited until evening to see if George came back. Finally, she rang his number again convinced he must be at home. A woman's voice answered.

"Hi, can I speak George Nazer please?"

"My uncle? I'm very sorry but he passed away a few weeks ago. I'm his niece Helen – can I help you?"

title: The Ipswich Mummy
description: An academic examines a forgotten Egyptian mummy in a provincial museum. What dread curse of a dark god does this ancient relic hold?
imageAlt: A skeletal tomb effigy lying beneath gothic stone arches
coverAlt: a skeletal tomb effigy lying beneath gothic stone arches
bodyHtml:
In the East Anglian town of Ipswich is a very average provincial museum. The red–brick Victorian building near the arboretum houses a variety of badly stuffed animals, a Narwhal's horn (which until recently was labelled as belonging to a unicorn) and a favourite amongst local children the small Egyptian collection.

Here in glass cases can be found a model Nile boat, canopic jars, sarcophagi and most exciting of all to the young and morbid the Ipswich Mummy – a wizened brown husk of a corpse its limbs twisted, eyes sewn shut, its mouth open as if in some silent scream. The left hand of the emaciated cadaver is missing but a little hair still clings to the scalp.

It was in this dusty corner of England that Susan Blake, a Californian postgraduate student of Egyptology from nearby Cambridge University laboured alone in that hot summer cataloguing the collection. The museum didn't have the reputation of larger institutions and Susan was of the opinion that all of the artefacts should be returned to Egypt but here was a very rare opportunity to study objects from the distant past at first hand.

The items had not been examined by an academic since the nineteen sixties and so perhaps there was also a chance of using modern knowledge and techniques to learn something new. And where to begin? Why with the mummy, of course, the most celebrated and mysterious of all the relics.

She started with the provenance of the Mummy. It had been brought to Paris by a French Hussar by the name of Lieutenant Lucien De Bie after Napoleon's Egyptian adventure. The cavalryman had died with tens of thousands of others in Bonaparte's disastrous invasion of Russian but his widow had lived a long life. The mummy had been auctioned upon her death and bought as lot No. 249 by Edward Bellingham an English medical student. The mummy then later appeared photographed at a number of King Tut parties in the roaring twenties, the body often (Susan shuddered with academic horror) dressed up and posed amongst the frivolities. Finally, it was entrusted to the museum by an anonymous donor in 1932. 

There were no grave goods accompanying the body so who the Mummy had been in life, what period they had lived in or even if they were an Ancient Egyptian at all was unknown. It had been speculated that the hand had been severed by medieval grave robbers to sell to a sorcerer but that was guesswork based on other examples.

Susan put on her mask, hairnet and gloves and set to work starting with the basics. She unlocked the case and gently lifted the light, shrivelled, brittle cadaver onto an examination table she had erected in the Egyptian room. Susan then picked up a surgical torch and began using her eyes and hands to minutely explore the body. From the skull, teeth and pelvis, she quickly ascertained they had been an adult male. There were some of the bindings still intact that might hold some clues – taking a sample for carbon dating would be a good start.

Suddenly she stopped. Shining a torch into the cavity of the open mouth she could see something in there – a foreign object stuck at the back of the throat. Susan selected a pair of tweezers and very, very gently tried to prize it out.  If it was stuck or too delicate she would have to wait for an x–ray. To her surprise, it loosened easily and came fully intact out with the tweezers. Her heart skipped a beat as she could clearly see it was a scrap of rolled–up papyrus. Professionalism told her to stop and contact other more experienced academics, but ambition drove her on and so as if performing heart surgery on a newborn she worked with two tweezers to open this tiny ancient scroll. 

Selecting a magnifying glass Susan could see to her delight extremely minute and faded but very neatly written hieroglyphics. It was composed in one of the most ancient forms but it must have been the work of a skilled scribe for the language was so clear that she could with very little effort to understand the marks.

The scroll read:

"I Ankhmahor, high priest of Nyarlathotep, servant of the Pharoah Nephren–Ka" – Nyarlathotep, it sounded like the name of a demon but given the title of a god thought Susan.  And Nephren–Ka an obscure ruler of the sixth dynasty. Nephren–Ka must have made himself unpopular because his name had been struct from almost all of his monuments by his successors. She continued reading. 

"–bids he whosoever should read my words–" ah the arrogance of men to assume the first person in the future to understand the scroll would be a he. "Let their body become as but an empty vessel to receive my seven souls."

"I have built thy temple to house the (something here about a shining gemstone of some kind) and slain the captives as the sacrifice, answer now my prayer oh my master the dweller?" No not dweller, Susan corrected herself more like a noun used for evil spirits – haunter would be a better translation. "Oh, my master the haunter of the dark aid me now so I may walk the earth again."

It's a spell or a curse thought Susan elated with the find. Also, we now have a name and some sort of date. Even if this was a hoax it was certainly something very exciting indeed. Just as she began to reach for the camera to take photos Susan started as she realised the time. 

That afternoon she had a date with Anna a hot Spanish nurse she had met in the one gay pub in Ipswich. They were meeting at the art cinema to watch Psycho – not Susan's sort of thing but Anna loved classic horror movies. If she didn't leave right away she'd be late. Quickly tidying up Susan glanced one last time at the mummy as she closed the door.

Impossible as it was Susan was almost certain the time–worn thing had moved, the right hand nearer the face and the head tilted back at another angle. Shaking her head to clear it she switched off the lights and locked the door. Quickly she hurried through the museum past the vases and stuffed animals. The place was completely deserted for who would visit such a stuffy place on such a glorious hot summer day?

Susan was glad of the sunshine and fresh air as she crossed Christ Church Park heading for the cinema. As she took in the glorious view of the English oaks and the Tudor mansion she daydreamed about her discovery and the papers it would allow her to write. The day was very hot indeed and as she tried to walk faster she soon became tired and dizzy. She increasingly felt light–headed and faint. Suddenly darkness covered her eyes and she stumbled forwards falling. A group of friends playing frisbee on the grass nearby saw her collapse, her body spasming and twitching on the floor and ran towards her to help.

Susan did not author any papers that summer but she was the subject of one. The monograph did not appear in any publications of Egyptology or archaeology but instead in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry.

The paper described a patient – Susan Blake, a young woman who had suffered a suspected seizure in a park. An ambulance was called and Ms Blake was conveyed to Ipswich General Hospital. Upon regaining consciousness the patient was unable to speak English, her mother tongue, but instead spoke in an unintelligible, perhaps invented language. CT and MRI scans showed an undamaged healthy brain and all other signs were normal.

When handed a pen and paper Ms Blake could not write in the Latin alphabet at all but instead drew long streams of intricate pictograms in the style of Egyptian hieroglyphics. This is not as strange as at first it might seem since the patient was a Cambridge postgraduate student well–versed in the arts of the ancient world. Ms Blake's university supervisor Dr Dorothy Heywood confirmed that the symbols were indeed part of a dead language. What is more, Dr Heywood explained that Ms Blake was attempting to convey in the writings that she was feeling in good health and eager to relearn the linguistic skills she had lost.

Psychologically the patient presented as well, despite having some long–term memory loss and having developed some eccentric phobias of modern technology.

With a speech coach and fellow academics helping with translation Ms Blake's English skills began to return and it was hoped that with more therapy she could return to normal life within a year.

Indeed after a year, Susan Blake was recovered enough to plan an extended trip to Egypt to see at first hand the monuments she was so familiar with. It should also come as no surprise that she wished to leave the Ipswich at that time for a shadow hung over the town. There had been through the winter a string of murders the victims including three sex workers but also that of a young Spanish nurse.  With the killer still at large and rumours of mutilations and black magic rituals, Ipswich had become a place of fear.

The last victim a local homeless man was slain a week before the young Egyptologist left the country and to this day the crimes have remained unsolved. Ipswich Museum remains open and you can still see the hideous and withered Mummy in its glass case, the body twisted and the mouth still open as if in agony. You can see it but you cannot hear the real Susan Blake silently screaming imprisoned for eternity inside that withered husk.

title: Vixen's Cry
description: Christmas and alone in a haunted Victorian house. Is that a Vixen’s cry in the dark or the screams of a child?
imageAlt: A weathered stone cherub carved into a monument
coverAlt: a weathered stone cherub carved into a monument
bodyHtml:
The lascivious cry of a vixen calling her lovers is an eerie sound to hear upon a winter's night; for the mating scream of the fox is indistinguishable from that of a child in great fear or pain. I have always disliked that uncanny screech but now I simply cannot bear to hear it at all, and I'll explain why.

It happened one Christmas when I was cat-sitting for my friends Rob and Jude. Jude is a partner in a city accountancy firm, and they own a very nice town house with a huge garden in the old Victorian centre of Walthamstow "the village" in estate agent speak. Like every Christmas the couple were to go sailing with friends in warmer climes but their two-house cats Siouxsie and Rocky needed to be fed and so they asked on Facebook if anyone could stay there for two weeks over the holidays.

That very week the boiler in my tiny flat had expired and despite frequent calls and emails my landlord was sluggardly in getting it repaired. After a few days of cold showers and wearing two jumpers indoors I jumped at the chance to stay a big comfortable home with a real open fire. My mother had passed away two years ago, and I was single and at a loose end anyhow. 

Rob, an affable schoolteacher with long hair and a big beard let me in and showed me around the place as his wife yelled at her inept underlings on a conference call in the lounge. I was to stay in the guest room at the back of the house overlooking the garden. And what a garden it was. There was a fine conservatory leading to a long lawn that ended in a small gate and then beyond that a great wild area. The previous summer at a barbecue Rob had explained that portion of the garden was too much for him and he'd left it to the foxes. Later that evening as if to illustrate his words a handsome red furry fellow had jumped over the wall and strolled straight past us. The animal turned to give us a foul look as if we were trespassing and then wandered off towards its den.

The house itself dated from the mid-nineteenth century with many fine original features including the tiled fireplace I coveted so much and a basement where Rob and Jules tinkered with brewing beer. The cats soon warmed to me after I had learnt how to feed them, the WIFI worked and a couple of very cosy pubs were but a short walk away. I could plan on a quiet but very comfortable Christmas. That night I shared a take-away curry with my hosts in front of a movie and then the next morning bid them bon voyage.

The first few days passed without incident – I did some Christmas shopping in the cute little shops on Orford Road and drank a pint in front of a roaring fire in the Castle. But as Christmas day approached an increase in the nocturnal noises from outside disturbed my sleep. From the wild end of the garden would come a terrible shriek like a banshee's wail – a set of cries that tore me from my slumbers and chilled my blood. It must have been a vixen in heat, but I'd swear by Christ somebody was being murdered out there.

With the calls came the nightmares. I dreamt I was lying at night in the bed in this guest room. The house was the same, but the room was different, thick curtains hung across the windows, the walls were covered in heavily patterned paper and in the gloom, I could make out the trapping of an old children's nursery. There was a wooden rocking horse and in my arms a porcelain doll with black eyes and a lacey dress. Nameless dread filled me and at the door stood the tall shadow of a man – a man I feared.

Alone in the big house and facing sleepless nights like these I began to avoid retiring to bed and stayed up later and later in the living room. I made my way through Rob's film collection drinking the homebrew beer they had left me. The cats snuggled up with me on the sofa for warmth and I could hear nothing from the garden – the lounge being at the front of the house and the racket of action movies covering anything I might have heard.

One night I fell asleep on the settee. My sleep was deep and completely without dreams, but I awoke the next day with my back, always my weak spot, in complete agony. After some fruitless stretches, I promised myself that I'd spend less time on the couch and only sleep in a proper bed.

That day was Christmas Eve and I had arranged to meet some friends in the village pub. We worked our way through mulled wine, ale and Irish whiskey until last orders after which I staggered back to the house. Mounting the staircase, I climbed upwards when I spied Siouxsie the tortoiseshell cat standing hissing upon the landing. She was facing the doorway of my room her back arched, her ears back, her fur standing right on end. I was too full of Dutch courage in that moment to be perturbed and chuckled "Strange cat," before stumbling onwards and throwing myself upon the bed into a drunken slumber.

But again, the nightmares came. Now I lay paralysed in my cot in the nursery as that shadow of that man I feared so much crept closer, stalking me with menace. I awoke in terror to the sound of a vixen keening the scream so human I sat bolt upright. Angry at being afraid and perhaps still somewhat inebriated I climbed out of bed and tore back the curtain to confront my vulpine tormentor.

The view of the garden clearly illuminated on that frosty night by the moon sobered me up immediately. Standing at the gateway between the tended garden and the portion left wild stood the figure of a child, a young girl with long hair covering her face, wearing just a white nightgown and something, a dolly perhaps, cradled in her arms.

At first, I stood motionless, my head spinning, body frozen to the spot when she let out a scream so awful, it chilled my blood. At that I turned tail and fled, slipping on the stairs and tumbling down hard.

When I came to, I was in pain, but nothing seemed broken. I stood up limping and considered my position. I did not believe in ghosts – either what I had seen in the garden was a child in distress who dearly needed help or a drunken hallucination.  Either way, I decided to immediately investigate to set my mind at ease. I threw on my coat and switched on my phone's flashlight as I fumbled for the conservatory key.

Gingerly I stepped into the garden, the night was bitterly cold, and I had to pull my coat tight around me as I advanced. As I approached the gateway, I called out "Hello? Do you need help?"

Then suddenly I caught site of a glimpse of the girl's white nightgown in the blackness of the overgrown field, she was about some twenty yards away. I passed through the gateway and stepped forward again calling out to her – half hoping for a reply and half fearing it.

She stood with her back to me pointing at the ground. As I approached again, I spoke "Hello? Do you-" before I could finish my words she turned and with the wan light of my torch I caught site of her face, or rather what was left of it. Where eyes should have been were just hollow voids in a bare white skull and her skeletal jaw hung open as she let out another terrible scream.

I dropped my phone and charged backwards running as fast as I could towards the house not looking back. With shaking hands, I locked the conservatory door, grabbed a bottle of vodka from the kitchen and barricaded the living room door, keeping the fire burning until morning light.

It was only at midday with the pale winter's sun giving me as much grey light as I could hope for, I dared to venture into the garden to retrieve my phone. It was just where I had dropped it, the battery completely drained. I looked around furtively before picking it up and then noticed something. In the daylight, I could now see clearly the spot the apparition had been pointing to. Amongst tangled weeds was a small cairn of stones piled up as if to mark something.

From that Christmas day, I spent the remaining nights in the lounge on the sofa wrapped in a duvet, the television constantly on. Finally, on the second of January, my hosts returned looking tanned and relaxed in contrast to my now pale haggard appearance. After Jude and Rob had regaled me with tails of sailing exploits and sea snakes, they asked me how things had been in the house. Haltingly I enquired if any other guests had noticed anything strange happening in the garden.

Jude answered, "No but we are always away at Christmas and you are the first person to stay over – normally we get a neighbour to feed the cats."

I didn't know what to say, "I think there is something at the back of the garden, buried."

"Buried?" asked Rob suddenly excited. Rob had read archaeology as an undergraduate and was still something of an amateur antiquarian. "This house is very old; I wouldn't be surprised if it had a few secrets to tell. Shall we have a look?"

"No, no it's probably nothing."

"Nonsense," Rob roared in his jovial way "I'll just get some tools"

In the garden, Rob pulled away the stones, and I broke the frozen ground with a pickaxe as he shovelled away the stones and soil. It wasn't very long before we hit something – an old luggage chest about four feet long in the shallow pit we had dug. The wooden timbers were rotted, and an old thickly rusted padlock held it shut. Rob struck the padlock with the pickaxe and the lock flew off. He started to prize it open and I turned my face away – I dreaded what we might find.

"Well, that's odd," said Rob.

I looked into the case fearing to see the bones of a child but the only item that lay in that buried chest was an old porcelain doll in the tatters of a lace dress.

title: The Exchange
description: An intelligence agent eavesdrops upon a suspected terrorist in an old telephone exchange building. But is he the only one listening?
imageAlt: A looming brick telephone exchange photographed from a low angle
coverAlt: a looming brick telephone exchange photographed from a low angle
bodyHtml:
Simon pulled over the car and checked his phone for the time and new messages. 1.21 am and nothing since the last text.

He looked up at the old telephone exchange across the street, a red brick building with art deco flourishes. Pale light shone out from a first–floor window the rest in darkness. When it had been new, back in the thirties perhaps, the place would have been full and busy. Girls working the switchboards and engineers keeping the machines running. Now the people were all gone, replaced by just a few cabinets of quietly humming machines, most of the rooms empty.  Exchanges couldn't be torn down or converted into flats because the cables often ran the whole length of the building. Drill a hole in the wrong place and a whole postcode could be cut off. And so they sat vacant, quiet monuments to the triumph of automation.

Simon selected one of many plastic ID cards from his glove compartment, grabbed his laptop bag and got out of the car. He strolled over to the metal doors and held the card up to the sensor. The lock buzzed open loudly and he pulled the door open and stepped inside. 

The security guard behind the desk almost jumped out of his chair.

"You look like you've seen a ghost" Simon joked. 

"There isn't any scheduled work." The security guard, an older man with dark eyes and white hair flustered gasped at his clipboard.

Alan Jordan, group engineering services," said Simon holding up the ID badge. 

"Group? This is an OpenReach building."

"If you call the main security desk you can give them my employee number."

"It's late can't you come back tomorrow?"

"Ring the main desk, they'll explain." Simon took off his lanyard and slid it across to the security guard.

The guard picked up the receiver and tired slowly dialled the number. 

"I've got a bloke here who says he's from group. Yes, I've got it here – six oh one four five seven three four zero."

There was a pause and then the voice on the other end of the line became excitable.

"Yes I understand," the guard hung up and looked at Simon suspiciously "Apparently I have to assist you in any way you want and not ask any questions. Nobody tells me anything." He passed the ID card back.

"Well it's best to check, you can't be too careful. Can you show me the server room."

"That's upstairs, I don't go up there at night."

"Really? Don't you patrol or something?"

"I have to stay here and watch the CCTV. It's up the stairs second on the right, no doubt your card will get you past the code." the guard opened the turnstile.

Unimpressed Simon strolled through, as he was walking away the guard stopped him. "One thing. Group is a holding company, why does it have engineering services?"

"You know what they said about not asking any questions."

The guard said nothing as Simon walked away into the stairwell. 

***

Stepping into the server room Simon could feel the static charge from the computers. The lights flickered for a moment and he thought he saw the silhouette of a woman by the window. But then the room was illuminated and it was gone – just a trick of the light.

He pulled his laptop from the case, running a cable between it and the cabinet. Then sitting down on a plastic chair he opened the computer resting it on his knees. After logging in he started the monitoring software. Disappointed with what he saw he flipped out a phone and spoke into it. 

"Hi David, it's Simon. Yes still encrypted I'm afraid...no don't do that not yet...he's getting lazy I can feel it, he's got to make a mistake soon...yes I'll call if anything happens."

He snapped the phone shut and looked back at the screen. Come on you bastard do something human preferably something with your real ID or bank card. Skype your mum, gamble online, watch some porn. It's dammed cold in here Simon thought – they must be running the air conditioning on full to keep the servers cool.

He wished he'd stopped for coffee and a Mars bar at the service station – no point in hurrying for this. As he stared at the screen his brain drifting off and then the lights flickered again.

Suddenly he heard a whisper in his ear a female voice "It's fun listening in on other people isn't it."

Simon started the laptop sliding to the floor, the lights coming on again. Nobody here he thought and then again he heard a sound, doors slamming out in the corridor. He stood up and walked over to the door, opened it and looked out, the corridor was pitch black, the lights out. He groped for a light switch, found it and switched it on. Nothing again.

And then a girl's giggle from down the hall, coming from one of the rooms. He walked towards it calling out "Hello you shouldn't be in here, this is BT property." Then there was a crash like a box falling over.

He threw open the door where the sound had come from. Just a storeroom full of boxes, papers spilling out of them. On the wall hung old photos showing the exchange in its glory days, rows of girls sitting at the switchboards. Simon had the funny feeling one of them was smiling at him.

His thoughts were interrupted by an electronic wail from the server room. He knew the noise immediately the target was communicating without encryption. He ran back to his abandoned machine and into the server room and that was when he saw her. She stood by the window looking out and said "Do you want to know what he says...it will be our little secret?"

Simon was ashen–faced as he left the building, on the way out the security guard said "Didn't think you'd want to be up there too long!"

title: The Black Monk
description: In a remote valley, a sinister presence dwells among the ruins of a medieval monastery, preying on victims across the centuries.
imageAlt: A ruined stone archway overgrown with vines
coverAlt: a ruined stone archway overgrown with vines
bodyHtml:
Part 1

If you are driving along the Riviera from France into Italy, you can turn left after Ventimiglia and head North into a valley in the foothills of the Alps. You will follow a stream along a winding road through picturesque villages with equally romantic names like Dolceacqua and Isolabona. You will see arched bridges and ruined castles clinging to the cliffs, but the best is yet to come. As you emerge from the tunnel at Isolabona, you will catch a glimpse of the hill village of A------.

A------ sits atop an incredibly steep, narrow spur of land surmounted by a church tower from which terracotta-rooved houses tumble down to the road. Its few narrow streets climb up to a small piazza at the top from which the whole of the valley can be viewed. Now whilst the village presents a beautiful sight to the modern tourist, aesthetic considerations were not the reason such a precipitous and defensible site was chosen.

Seven centuries ago, the villagers dwelt in an adjacent valley; their small farms clustered around a stone Benedictine monastery and its community of black-cowled monks.

The community was isolated away from the road, and far from the coast; in the winter months, the snow would cut off the valley completely, the wolves howling in the mountains. The monks ruled over their lay brothers and sisters with little interference from the outside; masters of their valley.

Occasionally rumours of heresy, of necromancy and murders reached other villages. The stories centred around Abbot Rainaldo, that he kept a secret copy of the Key of Solomon and commanded the spirits of the air. That he was a fiend and could change shape into that of a wolf. It was also said that travellers would sometimes enter the monastery as guests but were never seen to leave.

The bishop dismissed these tales, believing them to be gossip and the slander of the Baron who coveted the church land. And as long as the tithe of olives continued to be paid, the Bishop was happy to turn a blind eye.

Eventually the clamour grew amongst the peasants, and fearing the secular authorities would become involved, the old Bishop sent a commission. In the spring of the following year the austere Arch Deacon Pietro accompanied by a learned priest, servants and men-at-arms made the ascent up to the Monastery.

However, upon arrival in the valley, they were met not by Abbot Rainaldo but his funeral procession, for the leader of the community had died in his bed the very night before.

The hooded monks bore his heavy lead coffin to the old Romanesque monastery church to inter their leader in the crypt, solemnly chanting in Latin. As the tomb was sealed, the Arch Deacon noted that the sarcophagus was first bound with heavy iron chains, a strange custom indeed.

The following day Pietro began interviewing the monks, probing their beliefs and practices, questioning if they adhered to official church doctrine and if any laws of the land had been broken. Certain testimony and obscure figures in the marginalia of copied texts were enough to confirm the Arch Deacons suspicions. Some of the late Abbot's books and personal effects were burned. The monastery was dissolved; the monks dispersed to other Houses of God, the land sold to the Baron.

If the Bishop had hoped that was the end of the matter, he was to be disappointed. A number of witnesses claim to have seen the deceased Abbot Rainaldo sometimes as a man at other times in the form of a wolf. The common folk refused to approach the crumbling and overgrown monastery, openly declaring the place to be accursed.

Increasingly, the villagers left building new homes at the foot of the Baron's new castle upon a high ridge above the road and the old village was abandoned.

The desolate valley was left to the beast and the birds, visited only occasionally by brave shepherds. The Monastery became a roofless ruin, trees growing where monks had once prayed.

And so, it would have remained deserted and forgotten but for the rise of Benito Mussolini's Fascist party. Il Duce was keen to return the Italian people to the land and settle families on new farms on unused lots. A new road was constructed, houses built, and olive groves planted.

The villagers were back working the land in the place their ancestors had forsaken. One young family, Giovanni and Maria Lanteri, moved into a new stone farmhouse with their three young children not far from the woods that covered the Old Monastery. The couple worked building terraces and planting trees whilst the little ones played.

At first things went well. The youngest, little Tonio, timidly spoke of seeing "Il Vecchio", the old man dressed in black who watched the house at night, but the others dismissed this as a child's nightmare. In November, as the olives were harvested from the trees before the winter nights closed in. The wind whipped down from the mountains, slamming into the shutters of the house, and Maria told her husband that she could hear voices on the wind – like the sound of chanting. Giovanni said he heard no such thing but was keen to lock the doors when darkness fell and borrowed a shotgun from a neighbour.

In January Little Tonio failed to return from an errand; his parents searched the path and the woods calling his name until darkness defeated them. The next day the whole village was roused, beating the undergrowth and checking barns and wells. Some of the children said that a big wolf had taken Tonio, but that was impossible, for all the wolves were long gone. The boy was never found, and the next year the Lanteri family left Italy to join Giovanni's cousin in Argentina.

Part 2

Sergeant Hütter pointed to the map "The partisans will not attack the village from the road down there; one sniper in the church tower could hold out against an entire battalion. But from this path above here, besides the graveyard, A------ can be taken."

He wondered if the new recruits were listening to a word he said, the whole lot of them not worth one of the men he'd lost in Russia.

"The track leads along this ridge and down into the neighbouring valley." His finger traced the snaking contour lines on the map.

"We have intelligence that the partisans meet here at a ruined monastery." The finger now jabbed the paper. "We will make our way down there under the cover of night and set up ambush positions. When it gets dark, we move; stay alert, no talking. Let's give these Bolsheviks a surprise."

Bartos, a young, gangly recruit, was gazing wistfully at the view. Hütter despaired at keeping these boys alive. The squad should be nine strong, but now they were only seven, five of them youths in ill-fitting uniforms. Of the original unit, only two veterans remained: Schneider the machine gunner and Hütter himself.

"Bartos, wake up and check your equipment" he barked.

As the sunset behind the mountains, the frogs started their croaking chorus of "Egbert, Egbert" and the grenadiers began their patrol, keeping to the edges of the path. Hütter took the lead; behind him, the boys stumbled along whilst Schneider, a giant of a man, carried the hefty machine gun across his shoulder like Jesus bearing the cross.

The path led steeply upwards, zig-zagging up and over the hill, before turning downwards again. Hütter could hear the laboured breathing of the recruit bearing Schneider's ammunition. There was enough moonlight to see the valley – no village here, just a few scattered farmhouses, terraced olive groves and tangled woods.

Suddenly Hütter held his hand up – the others stopped as their leader crept forward. The Sergeant could see two small moving lights ahead in the undergrowth - lit cigarettes, perhaps? Deliberately and smoothly, he pulled the bolt back on his Schmeiser and stepped into the shadow of a tree. The lights flashed again, and he almost laughed with relief – the dancing sparks were fireflies.

Grinning, he beckoned the others forward, for now he could see a fork in the path leading to the monastery. Turning off, he picked up the pace now that their objective was close.

And then he could see it. A broken shell of a church on the edge of an escarpment, withered vines clinging to its shattered walls. Hütter clambered through an archway and looked inside. Others might have marvelled at the age of the ruin and wondered why it had been deserted, but as a Sergeant of the Wehrmacht he saw only one thing: a ready-made strongpoint. He turned to the others and spoke in a whisper, "Schneider and Flür, machine gun here in this archway covering the path. The rest stay back there in the treeline with me. Now it is easy to shoot a comrade in the dark, so don't fire until you are certain of a target."

The position was almost perfect for an ambush, and the partisans were nothing but a ragtag rabble of farmers, but the Sergeant felt uneasy. There was something wrong about this place, something that reminded him of the smell of death on a battlefield.

They waited, staring into the dark, trying to stay awake and concentrate; the frogs ceased their monotonous chanting, and the dogs stopped barking as silence filled the valley.

Hütter flinched as he could just make out a dark shape moving along the path. As it approached, he could see a solitary cowled figure the face covered, perhaps a priest? Something about the person's movements suggested an old man. What was this ancient fool doing roaming abroad at the midnight hour? Perhaps the partisans had sent him ahead to check the monastery was safe. If so, Hütter would take him prisoner and make him talk.

The hooded man limped towards the ruin directly facing the archway and the hidden machine gun. It was summer night in Italy but as the wind picked up, the Sergeant felt the cold of the winter war. The old man lifted his head to look directly into the archway.

Someone gasped, "Mein Gott" and then everything was sound and light as the machine gun opened fire. The muzzle was wreathed in flame, and tracer bullets sped like fireworks through the night. The men were dazzled and deafened by the gunfire, and Hütter's bellowed order of "Ceasefire!" was ignored by the gunner. What the hell was Schneider shooting at?

Abruptly the firing stopped; they must have used the whole belt.

"Anyone hit?"

No answer.

Hütter crawled out towards the spot the old man had been, where he expected to find an eviscerated corpse. At that range Schneider couldn't miss, and the machine gun would have cut anyone in half. But as he inched closer and his eyes readjusted to the dark, he realised the old man was gone.

"Scheiße!"

The ambush had been revealed, as the whole valley would have heard the gunfire and any partisans fled. But where was the old priest? Even if by some miracle he had not been hit, he could not have got far.

Hütter's thoughts were interrupted by sobbing coming nearby. "Whoever the fuck that is shut your mouth before I give you something to cry about."

"Sarge – Bartos is gone; he was just to the right of me," another voice "His rifle is here, but he's gone."

"Bartos, stop taking a shit and get back to your post", Hütter yelled.

"Bartos!"

But only the wind answered.

Part 3

I am sitting now, writing this in the holiday home of my wife's mother in February, looking out over the valley. They say it never snows in A------, and yet is snowing outside, and a thick white blanket covers the hills. The houses built under Mussolini are now peopled by Dutch and English retirees, but few will be here in Winter. Long forgotten, the ruins of the monastery still stand among tangled trees a few hundred yards from this house.

Wolves have returned to the Alps, and some say they have been spotted this far South chasing the deer and wild pigs. It is getting dark outside, and the wind is picking up. And as I look out into the gloom, do my eyes trick me, or is it that cowled figure in black I see limping through the snow?

title: Correspondence Chess
description: Can a gameboard be haunted or possessed? And if you play against an opponent from the netherworld, what are the stakes?
imageAlt: A chess knight and queen on a worn board
coverAlt: a chess knight and queen on a worn board
bodyHtml:
Unfortunately, it happens sometimes, and more often these days, that an elderly tenant dies with no next of kin. In these sad, lonely cases, the council has to enter the property and clear it of possessions. When I say the council, I mean Tracy and me, who deal with this sort of thing amongst our many other tasks.

On that grey autumn morning, we waited in the rain as the locksmith opened up. The small, narrow house was the same as all the others in the street, the usual council house. The door popped open, the locksmith stepped back, his work done, and we entered.

When you get inside one of these places, you don’t know what to expect. Some of the tenants were hoarders in life, and there is rubbish and broken furniture piled high in every room. Some have kept animals or fed pigeons, and the place is full of filth and vermin whilst other places are clean and homely. And sometimes, as on this occasion, the property is depressingly empty, with bare walls and a few meagre possessions.

The deceased was Istvan Szabo, an old man who’d been born in Hungary but had fled to the UK many decades ago. Istvan had clearly died with very little to his name - one ancient TV, a signed black-and-white photograph of the Hungarian national football team, some unopened tins of pilchards, old clothes, a pile of chess magazines and a battered chessboard.

As Tracy threw clothes into bin bags upstairs, I stopped to look at the board. I play beginner chess online and have an amateur’s interest in the game. I recognised the pieces were laid out in the opening of a game - white had advanced the king’s pawn to E4, and black had responded with the Sicilian defence. Had the old man been practising alone, or did he have a friend on the estate we didn’t know about - a chess partner who for some reason hadn’t come forward?

Suddenly, on a whim, I made a move for white, picking up a knight and swinging it out to F3. I don’t know why I did it - perhaps I wanted to make a gesture of respect to the dead man, or maybe I was just too tempted by the position? I then turned to unplug the television, but as I did so I heard a scraping noise from the board behind me.

Glancing over my shoulder, I expected to see Tracy in the room, but she wasn’t there, and I could hear her singing as she worked upstairs. Glancing again at the chessboard, I noticed something had changed. Black had responded to my knight’s move by pushing forward another pawn. But of course, that was impossible; I was alone in the room. I must have been mistaken, but then the board made no sense, Black would have made an extra move. However, to be sure, I shoved a pawn forward, tempting Black to capture it, before heaving the TV out of the house and into the back of the van.

When I returned, I went straight to the board to set my mind at ease that nothing had moved. But once again something had changed. Not only had black’s pawn moved diagonally, sitting in the square I had just moved to, but my white pawn had been removed and placed neatly beside the board.

Not trusting my senses, I pulled out my phone and took a photo of the board. And then, for good measure, I switched to video mode, filming the board as I responded to black’s move by taking his pawn with my knight. I waited for something to happen, eager to record anything odd. But then I heard Tracy shout from the bedroom, “Oi Dave, give us a hand to shift this will yah!”

Grumbling to myself, I headed upstairs to help carry. After a few minutes of huffing and puffing down the stairs with boxes, I got a chance to check the board again. This time I had a photograph to compare the current state of play with. And without a doubt, something had moved - black had developed one of his knights.

Now I was certain either I was suffering from a delusion or the pieces were moving themselves. If I had told Tracy, she would have assumed the former - but I was sure there was some kind of technology or a magic trick at play - something with magnets and a computer, perhaps. Quickly I swiped the pieces up and folded the board, placing them inside the box. As I did so, I noticed the old, worn box had a faded print on it - an illustration of a man in a turban and furs sitting behind a cabinet full of cogs and gears, playing chess.

Now I can honestly say I have never swiped anything when on one of these jobs for two reasons - firstly, it just wouldn’t feel right, and secondly, most of it is old junk. But on this occasion curiosity overcame me; I needed to know what was going on. I wanted to be alone to examine and test the board. And so quickly I sneaked the small box into my backpack and got on with clearing the place.

That evening in my flat I took the board out and had a long look, taking my time scrutinising every detail. The pieces were hollow, made of some early plastic, with felt bases peeling off from the bottom. I peered inside several of them but found them completely empty. The board itself was made of cardboard with dog-eared corners and coffee stains - it didn’t seem thick enough to hold any mechanism other than perhaps the latest thinnest silicon chips.

On the reverse was what looked like a different game. Ten circles connected by interleaved lines arranged in a geometric pattern. Inside the circles and on the lines were what looked like Hebrew letters - some old Eastern European Jewish board game, perhaps? Had Szabo been Jewish? There was nothing in the paperwork or his home to suggest that, but what did I really know about the old fella?

Perplexed, I set up the game from the photograph and memory as it had been in the dead man’s house. This time I tried something different - an illegal move. I picked up a rook and moved it over some pawns to take black’s queen. Suddenly there was a loud knocking noise, as if somebody had rapped their knuckles on the coffee table I was playing on. Startled and slightly embarrassed, I quickly moved the pieces back into place. Feeling I should make amends, I now made another legal and sensible move for white and waited. Nothing happened...of course it only moved when I wasn’t looking. I shuffled off to the kitchen to make some supper - letting the board have some privacy.

Now, as expected, when I returned, the position had again changed, and that was how I became drawn into the game. Over the course of that week, I’d make a move every night after work. Sometimes I’d talk out loud to the board, going through the game and how I understood it was developing - trying to draw it into some more conversation. Sometimes I’d address it as friend, other times as Istvan. But it never replied and made no sound after that first fearful knock, letting its playing do the talking.

And what play. Soon the board led by a bishop; I couldn’t castle and was pinned back into my own half. I’d really have to improve if I were going to beat it. And so, things went until she arrived.

That Thursday night I had just climbed into bed after a takeaway curry, my mind still full of the game and how I could avoid losing when the doorbell rang. It was late, about half twelve, and I wondered who it could be - a neighbour in trouble or something more sinister? I threw on my dressing gown, put the chain on, and opened the door a few inches. Standing outside was a small pale young woman dressed all in black, old-fashioned clothes. She looked aggrieved.

“David Johnson?” she asked, her voice clear with a slight Eastern European accent.

“Yes?”

“You have something that is not yours. You are going to lose, and you do not know what the stakes are.”

“Now look here, how did you get my address? I don’t know what you want; it’s late, and I’m not letting you in.”

“There isn’t much time, he is going to-”

I didn’t let her finish slamming the door in her face, pulling the bolt across and retreating back into my flat. She didn’t ring again but instead dropped something through the letterbox. It was a business card. On one side was printed a word in Hebrew script, a telephone number and an address in Seven Sisters. On the other, written in biro, was simply NxF2 - a chess notation for a knight taking a pawn on the square F2.

Somewhat worried, I switched on the lights in the living room and surveyed the game again. So, if I moved my queen as I planned and then black took the pawn on F2 with his knight.
